opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the core value is really about decoupling. Right now, if you're a company that wants to use agents seriously, you end up making a bet on a specific harness, whether that's Claude Code, Codex, or something else, and then everything you build around it, your tools, your context, your evaluation setup, your governance, gets tied to that one choice. A common API lets you separate the "what the agent is doing for my business" layer from the "which harness and which model is running it" layer.

That matters for a few reasons. First, the field is moving incredibly fast. The best harness for a given task six months from now might not be the one you picked today, and you want to be able to swap or mix them without rewriting your whole stack. We saw the same thing with data systems: people really valued open formats and common interfaces because it meant they weren't locked into one engine, and you got healthy competition on quality and cost.

Second, it makes evaluation and comparison actually possible. If every harness exposes the same way to give it a task, give it tools, and observe what it did, then you can run the same workload across them and measure accuracy, cost, and latency in an apples-to-apples way. Without that, people mostly pick based on vibes.

Third, and I think this is underrated, is the enterprise side: security, permissions, auditing, observability. If agents are going to touch real data and real systems, you need one consistent place to say what an agent is allowed to access and to trace what it did. You don't want to re-implement that governance for every harness separately.

And finally, it's good for the ecosystem. Tool builders and people building context or memory systems can target one interface and work everywhere, rather than writing N integrations. So, to me, it's similar to what SQL or standard storage formats did for data: the interface becomes the stable thing, and the implementations underneath can keep getting better.

r001.rationale: It says a common API lets companies swap or mix harnesses without rewriting their stack, but does not identify the burden of keeping up with changing harness APIs or a maintained interface removing that burden from orchestrator developers.

r002.rationale: It discusses common interfaces for tools and context systems, but does not state that developers can connect their own user interface to a common-interface server.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core value is that it decouples the thing you're actually building from the particular harness you happened to start with. Right now, if you build a workflow or a tool integration on top of Claude Code, or on top of Codex, you're writing against that harness's quirks: how it exposes tool calls, how it manages context, how it reports progress, how permissions work. And the moment you want to try a different model or a different agent runtime, you're rewriting a lot of plumbing that has nothing to do with your actual problem.

We saw this same pattern in data infrastructure. Spark got a lot of adoption partly because it gave people one API that could run across different storage systems and clusters, so you weren't locked into one vendor's stack to get your job done. Agent harnesses are at a similar moment. The models are changing every few months, the harnesses are changing just as fast, and the people who are building real applications on top of them need some stable surface to target.

So a common API does a few concrete things. First, it makes evaluation honest. If I can run the same task, with the same tools and the same observability hooks, across two harnesses, I can actually compare them instead of comparing my implementation of each. That matters a lot for enterprises trying to decide what to adopt. Second, it lets the ecosystem build shared infrastructure: logging, tracing, guardrails, cost controls, sandboxing. Nobody wants to build those five times. Third, it lowers the risk of adopting any of this. A lot of companies are hesitant to go deep on agents because they're worried they'll pick the wrong horse. A common layer makes that bet much less scary.

The caveat I'd add is that the API has to be at the right level of abstraction. If it's too low, you've just standardized the message format and everyone still diverges on the things that matter. If it's too high, you flatten away the real differences between harnesses, which are often where the value is. The interesting design work is finding the layer where the integration surface is shared but the harnesses can still compete on how well they plan, recover from errors, and manage long-running context. I think we're still figuring that out, but the fact that people are converging on the question at all is a good sign.

r001.rationale: The response describes harness-specific APIs and quirks changing, forcing developers to rewrite plumbing when switching runtimes, and says a common API provides a stable surface that removes that burden.

r002.rationale: The response mentions shared infrastructure and integrations, but does not state that developers can plug their own user interface into the common-interface server.

astra-6.text:
I think the core value is that you can separate the application you’re building from the particular agent harness underneath it. These harnesses do a lot more than call a model—they manage tools, context, and the loop of taking actions and looking at results. If each one has a different interface, you end up coupling your application to those choices.

A common API lets you try Claude Code or Codex on the same task, evaluate which works better, and switch without rewriting the integration. It also makes it easier to take advantage of improvements as those systems evolve. You still want access to their unique capabilities, but you shouldn’t have to rebuild the basic plumbing every time you want to try another one.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the core value is that you can separate the application from the agent harness. If you’re building a product that delegates work to a coding agent, you don’t want to rebuild that integration for every harness. You want a common way to submit a task, provide context, get progress updates, and collect the result.

That doesn’t mean every agent has to work the same way internally. They can make different choices about planning, tools, and context management. But a shared interface lets you try those alternatives, evaluate them on your actual workload, and switch as they improve. The harness becomes something you can choose based on how well it does the job.
